title: El coche prestado y el raspón en Guadalajara

dialogue.speaker: Diego
dialogue.spanish: Oye, Fernanda, no manches... Acabo de bajar al estacionamiento y vi que mi coche tiene un raspón enorme en la defensa trasera.
dialogue.english: Hey, Fernanda, no way... I just went down to the parking lot and saw that my car has a huge scratch on the back bumper.

slang.actualMeaning: No way! / You've got to be kidding me!

dialogue.speaker: Fernanda
dialogue.spanish: Ay, Diego, te iba a decir ahorita que saliéramos. Ayer que me lo prestaste para ir por las cosas de mi chamba, un poste estaba súper pegado en la rampa.
dialogue.english: Oh, Diego, I was going to tell you right now when we went out. Yesterday when you lent it to me to pick up my work stuff, a pillar was super close on the ramp.

slang.example: Conseguí una nueva chamba cerca de mi casa.

dialogue.speaker: Diego
dialogue.spanish: ¿Y pensabas hacerte pato o qué? Sabes que lo acabo de sacar del taller hace dos semanas.
dialogue.english: And were you planning to play dumb or what? You know I just got it out of the repair shop two weeks ago.

slang.example: No te hagas pato, te toca lavar los platos.

dialogue.speaker: Fernanda
dialogue.spanish: ¡Claro que no me iba a hacer pato! Ya hablé con el taller de mi tío Memo en Zapopan. Dice que mañana mismo lo pule y lo pinta por mil quinientos pesos.
dialogue.english: Of course I wasn't going to play dumb! I already spoke with my uncle Memo's body shop in Zapopan. He says tomorrow he'll buff and paint it for fifteen hundred pesos.

dialogue.speaker: Diego
dialogue.spanish: Bueno, menos mal... Pero esa lana la pones tú, ¿eh? Y me llevas a mi oficina en la mañana mientras lo arreglan.
dialogue.english: Well, thank goodness... But you're paying that cash, alright? And you're driving me to my office in the morning while they fix it.

slang.example: Ahorré una buena lana para las vacaciones.

dialogue.speaker: Fernanda
dialogue.spanish: Trato hecho. Yo pago todo el taller y encima te compro tu torta ahogada para que se te baje el coraje.
dialogue.english: Deal. I'll pay for the whole shop and on top of that I'll buy you your drowned pork sandwich so you stop being mad.

questions.question: Why is Diego upset with Fernanda at the start of the conversation?
options: He found a big scratch on the back bumper of his car after lending it to her
She returned his car with an empty gas tank
She forgot to pick him up from the repair shop
She parked his car in a tow-away zone
questions.explanation: Diego saw a huge scratch ('un raspón enorme') on the rear bumper ('la defensa trasera') after lending his car to Fernanda yesterday.

questions.question: How did the car get scratched, and what plan did Fernanda already arrange?
options: She scraped a tight pillar on a ramp; her Uncle Memo's shop in Zapopan will buff and paint it tomorrow for 1,500 pesos
Another driver hit her in traffic; her insurance will pay 3,000 pesos
A shopping cart hit the door; she bought touch-up paint for 500 pesos
She backed into a tree; Diego's mechanic will fix it next week
questions.explanation: Fernanda scraped a tight pillar on a ramp and arranged for her Uncle Memo's body shop in Zapopan to buff and paint it tomorrow for 1,500 pesos.

questions.question: In addition to Fernanda paying for the repair, what else does Diego demand—and what food does Fernanda offer him?
options: She must drive him to his office in the morning, and she offers to buy him a 'torta ahogada'
She must wash his car, and she offers him street tacos
She must lend him her bicycle, and she offers to buy him coffee
She must pay his parking fee, and she offers to cook dinner
questions.explanation: Diego insists she pay the cash ('esa lana la pones tú') and drive him to his office in the morning, and she offers him a 'torta ahogada'.

questions.question: Slang Side Quest: What do the Mexican idioms 'hacerse pato', 'la chamba', and 'la lana' mean?
options: 'Hacerse pato' = play dumb; 'la chamba' = work/job; 'la lana' = money/cash
'Hacerse pato' = drive fast; 'la chamba' = party; 'la lana' = sweater
'Hacerse pato' = apologize; 'la chamba' = garage; 'la lana' = paint
'Hacerse pato' = get angry; 'la chamba' = school; 'la lana' = debt
questions.explanation: In Mexican Spanish, 'hacerse pato' means to play dumb, 'la chamba' is work/job, and 'la lana' is money/cash!
